reasoning_traces.think:
The core insight of Causal E-Process Theory lies in recognizing that standard predictive scoring fails when predictions influence the very outcomes they describe. This leads to a fundamental redefinition of how we measure skill: instead of relying on fixed likelihoods, we must consider the impact of interventions on the outcome distribution. The e-process \mathcal{E}_t = p_t(Y_t \mid do(\iota_t))/m_t(Y_t) captures this by incorporating the causal effect of the forecast itself. When the system is reactive—such as markets responding to picks—the likelihood ratio becomes a function of both the outcome and the intervention. This necessitates a shift from traditional Bayesian updating to a framework where the null hypothesis is defined relative to a set of admissible interventions I_t. The resulting theory ensures that even in such feedback-rich environments, one can still perform valid statistical inference. The impossibility theorem in Part II further highlights that without additional structure (like randomized publication), no test can reliably distinguish between genuine skill and mere echo. Thus, the framework introduces a dual approach: one that validates causal skill through e-processes and another that circumvents the reflexive limit via randomized mechanisms.

reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: Opposing agents include the market, which responds to forecasts, and the forecaster, who may misinterpret success due to feedback effects. The framework models these interactions by treating the forecaster as part of the system, thus requiring a causal lens to disentangle signal from noise. reasoning_traces.cross_layer_veto: Anti-collinearity arises when the same information is used to both generate and validate predictions. Leakage occurs if the e-process is not properly conditioned on the intervention. Veto conditions require that all interventions be non-anticipatory and that the null model remains invariant under the action of the admissible set.
